assumptions.summary: Near-future EV and CV parameters are assumed to represent their features.
No new vehicle type is assumed to disrupt the EV/CV market.
EV means pure electric vehicle; hybrids and hydrogen fuel cells are excluded.
The paper assumes its used data are accurate and reliable.
A vehicle is treated as a stationary ground-level point source.
Wind is parallel to the x-axis, uniform, and invariant.
Emission mass is conserved during dispersion.
Pollutant concentration is normally distributed in y and z, and the ground does not absorb pollutants.
Power-station emissions are assigned to EVs for the comparison boundary.
EV drivers never return to conventional vehicles.
Average EV purchase rate is approximately invariant.
EVs can replace CVs and attract new users.
EVs are assumed to enter the market completely in 2015 for the China example.
Fleet-share scenarios hold the current vehicle count and fixed annual fuel/electricity use.
AHP pairwise judgments are assumed to represent cost, efficiency, pollution, safety, and EV-development priorities.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Table 1 supplies RAV4 EV/RAV4 purchase, fees, energy use, mileage, maintenance, battery price, and battery mileage.
Table 2 prints lifecycle-cost components and totals for the two RAV4 variants.
Table 4 supplies HC, CO, NO2, CO2, and SOx values for gasoline, thermal-electric, and natural-gas-electric cases.
The paper assigns normalized AP weights 6.11, 3.86, and 1 to the three source cases.
Table 5 supplies average AP and GHG factors for CVs and EVs.
Table 7 supplies 2004-2009 world vehicle counts and supports a rough 1.15-billion estimate.
Table 8 supplies inside/outside noise at 35 and 50 km/h under uniform speed and acceleration.
China private-car history for 1985-2008 is mentioned as the curve-fitting basis but not reproduced.
Figures 8 and 9 supply WTT, TTW, and overall efficiency chains for CVs and EVs.
The resource calculation uses r=0.7, c=1500 kg/year, a=8, e=20, and 0.3 kg coal/kWh.
The Norton forecast supplies 2045 counts of 1.95 billion EVs and 0.49 billion CVs.
Table 9 supplies the O-C pairwise judgment matrix.
Table 10 supplies alternative priorities and lambda_max, CI, and CR for five matrices.
The final calculation scales 3450 billion kWh by w2 into four generation quantities.

language_observations.summary: Human style comes from a blunt feasibility question, mirrored task-method bullets, component-by-component derivations, conditional table readings, explicit base-model failure, concrete figure ranks, actor-separated recommendations, and forecast-to-resource handoffs rather than connector density.

introduction moves from converging pressures to a feasibility question: Combine several real-world pressures, state the apparent advantage, insert the upstream burden that complicates it, and end with a direct feasibility question.

plain task bullets are followed by a one-to-one method map: List the requested outputs in ordinary language, then mirror them with one named model or calculation per task before detailed modeling begins.

assumptions define scope now and defer model-specific premises to the model that needs them: State global scope restrictions first, then explicitly postpone specialized assumptions until the corresponding model is introduced.

a consumer-facing total is assembled from named cost components: Choose the decision perspective, enumerate acquisition, operation, recovery, and externality components, derive each locally, and combine them into one comparable total.

table reading states the unfavorable headline and then names conditions under which the comparison changes: Read the common metric, acknowledge the current disadvantage, isolate a compensating subcost, and state the parameter conditions needed for the alternative to become attractive.

sensitivity prose perturbs inputs, ranks responses, and connects the ranking to a future mechanism: State the perturbation rule, report response percentages, rank the inputs, then explain which external trend could move the comparison over time.

analysis shifts emissions from the tailpipe boundary to the generation boundary: Begin with the visible local benefit, name the upstream process that reintroduces burden, define the comparison boundary, and separate source technologies.

a spatial model is introduced through purpose, assumptions, formula, parameters, and simulation: Name the spatial question, justify the selected model, list the idealizations, display the governing equation, define symbols, substitute parameters, and state what the simulation will reveal.

each figure is read as a rank and then converted into a source-selection action: Describe the plotted reach or magnitude, rank alternatives on the same visual scale, and connect the ordering to the next technology choice.

two incomplete base models are explained before being combined: Introduce the external and internal mechanisms separately, explain what drives each, state that neither suffices, and combine them in one equation before solving.

a single-innovation diffusion model is modified into a two-technology substitution model: Simplify the base solution into a reusable adoption function, add switching assumptions and entry time, write incumbent and entrant equations, and hand future counts to downstream calculations.

weakness prose names the missing input or imprecise algorithm and proposes a concrete repair: Identify the unavailable data or unstable coefficient, explain how it affects the result, and name the additional data or alternative estimation method that would improve it.

model results are translated into separate government and manufacturer actions: Name the stakeholder, cite the model result that matters to that actor, identify the lever under its control, and state the action in operational terms.

efficiency diagrams feed a transparent resource-accounting chain: Read comparable well-to-wheel efficiencies, define per-vehicle conversion formulas, apply market-share scenarios, and hand total electricity demand to generation planning.

AHP moves from a benefit goal through criteria and alternatives to an explicit generation mix: Define the decision goal, expose criteria and alternatives in a hierarchy, show judgment matrices and consistency checks, then convert the weight vector into physical generation quantities.

unresolved_questions: The lifecycle-cost sign convention is not fully explained in prose; the visual formula subtracts reclamation income while OCR text can suggest addition.
Fuel cost uses total mileage and per-100-km consumption without a visible division by 100, creating a dimensional and scale risk.
Charging cost likewise multiplies mileage by per-100-km consumption without a visible 100-km conversion.
Battery replacement count is treated as a continuous ratio and does not specify rounding, residual battery life, discounting, or replacement timing.
Environmental costs are represented by hypothetical taxes rather than measured damages, and those terms are later dropped from the numerical comparison.
The RAV4 comparison does not report discount rate, price year, currency normalization, financing, insurance, degradation, or uncertainty.
Table 2 appears inconsistent with the stated annual maintenance inputs and 500,000-km fuel calculation; the arithmetic is not independently reconciled.
The 5% one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis is local and does not test interactions, distributions, scenario ranges, or sign errors.
A moving road fleet is idealized as a stationary ground-level point source with uniform wind, no deposition, and no terrain or chemistry.
The Gaussian formula uses fixed sigma values rather than distance- and stability-dependent dispersion parameters.
The mass-conservation integral is displayed without finite domain, source height, reflection term, or numerical implementation details.
The plume simulations use circle counts derived from normalized coefficients, but axes, time, emission rate, and mapping from coefficients to circles are not fully defined.
Power-station emissions are assigned to EVs as direct emissions without transmission losses, generation dispatch, regional mix, temporal charging, or lifecycle boundaries.
Scenario totals multiply fixed per-kilometer factors by vehicle count but omit distance traveled and therefore do not preserve the stated g/km units.
AP combines unlike pollutants through an unexplained normalization and weighting scheme.
The 1.15-billion vehicle estimate is extrapolated from a short table without uncertainty, fleet-class definition, or scenario year alignment.
Figures 5 and 6 are internal scenario charts, not observations; the conclusion overstates improvements in dispersion speed and affected area.
Noise and health sections use small cited tables and qualitative claims without exposure duration, population, charging-field measurement, or causal validation.
Battery toxicity is described qualitatively, but chemistry, collection rate, recycling pathway, dose, and lifecycle comparison are absent.
Bass-type diffusion is used without documenting the historical series, fitted parameter values, residuals, confidence intervals, or out-of-sample performance.
The text states m>0 where the model uses market capacity M, and the stated parameter constraints are not tied to estimation.
The inflection-point expression is poorly typeset and is not carried into any numerical check.
Norton substitution assumes irreversible switching, constant purchase rate, a fixed 2015 market entry, and attraction of new users without stress tests.
The forecast axes and units are not fully documented; claims for 2028, 2042, 2045, and 2060 are not benchmarked against held-out data.
The proposed genetic-algorithm repair is not implemented, tuned, or compared with the curve-fitting method.
The crude-saving calculation assumes every replaced vehicle consumes 1.5 tons of fuel annually and treats gasoline-plus-diesel yield as a direct conversion ratio.
The electricity calculation uses a fuel-consumption proxy for travel and does not propagate efficiency, charging loss, mileage distribution, or generation loss.
Coal results are printed as kilograms although fleet-scale electricity implies much larger units; this is a severe scale or unit error.
AHP pairwise judgments have no respondent, elicitation process, uncertainty interval, or sensitivity analysis.
The aggregate consistency formula and weights a_j are not defined clearly enough for independent replay from the paper alone.
AHP weights are treated as physical generation proportions even though the criteria mix preferences, impacts, safety, and development without capacity constraints.
The final allocation omits load shape, dispatchability, resource limits, grid reliability, capital cost, emissions lifecycle, regional feasibility, and policy authority.

writing_logic.summary: urban environment + oil cost + battery progress -> apparent EV promise -> upstream fossil-generation complication -> feasibility question
four requested outputs -> page 3 one-to-one approach bullets -> named LCC, plume, Norton, resource, and AHP methods
global scope assumptions -> consumer lifecycle-cost perspective -> four components -> equations -> RAV4 data -> common total
unfavorable current LCC result -> compensating operating advantage -> 5% perturbation -> sensitivity ranking -> future cost mechanism
tailpipe-zero claim -> upstream generation boundary -> AP/GHG split -> spatial dispersion question
plume purpose -> idealizing assumptions -> coordinate diagram -> equations -> source cases -> ranked plots
model strengths and weaknesses -> simpler fleet-share equations -> scenario charts -> local environmental conclusion
air/noise benefits -> battery and charging risks -> health bridge -> future adoption question
external model -> internal model -> neither sufficient -> combined Bass model -> closed-form adoption function
single-innovation function -> switching assumptions -> Norton incumbent/entrant equations -> fitted forecast -> plotted milestones
forecast result -> explicit data and coefficient weaknesses -> possible GA repair -> stakeholder-specific levers
government levers separated from manufacturer levers -> efficiency diagrams -> per-vehicle resource formulas
current-share resource scenarios -> Norton 2045 handoff -> future fleet resource total -> electricity-demand input
benefit goal -> five criteria -> four alternatives -> pairwise matrices -> consistency -> weights -> physical generation quantities
